name: AI and Authorship
title: AI and Authorship
answer: AI and authorship examines how generative systems change who or what can be credited as an author, covering human-AI collaboration, disclosure norms, originality, and the integrity of scholarly and creative records. It spans research papers, books, code, journalism, and artistic works where language models draft, revise, or generate content. The topic also includes questions of whether an AI can hold copyright, be named as co-author, or bear responsibility for errors and fabrication. For research integrity, it addresses ghost authorship, undisclosed machine assistance, and the reliability of author contributions.

sections.body: AI and authorship examines how generative systems change who or what can be credited as an author, covering human-AI collaboration, disclosure norms, originality, and the integrity of scholarly and creative records. It spans research papers, books, code, journalism, and artistic works where language models draft, revise, or generate content. The topic also includes questions of whether an AI can hold copyright, be named as co-author, or bear responsibility for errors and fabrication. For research integrity, it addresses ghost authorship, undisclosed machine assistance, and the reliability of author contributions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large language models and multimodal systems accessed through commercial APIs, open-weight models, or institutional deployments, often with retrieval and citation plugins. Authorship workflows may involve drafting assistants, summarizers, translators, and code generators embedded in word processors or research notebooks. The site's library of 135 research papers and 803 scientific models provides a reference base for studying these systems, but the infrastructure itself is the model plus the human review layer around it. Logging and version control are part of the practical stack when authorship claims need to be audited.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: How the work is done includes prompt design, iterative drafting, human editing, and disclosure of which parts were machine-generated. Researchers and editors compare AI-assisted text against style, factual, and citation checks, and use provenance tools to detect undisclosed synthetic prose. Authorship analysis often involves close reading of contribution statements, revision histories, and model outputs rather than a single automated score. The site's 10,767 extracted claims and 674 glossary terms support structured comparison of how different papers describe machine involvement.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on attribution, accountability, and the conditions under which AI use must be declared. Publishers, funders, and institutions set policies on whether AI can be listed as an author, usually requiring human authors to take responsibility for all content. Risks include fabricated references, plagiarism, loss of authorial voice, and disputes over credit when a model contributes substantive text or ideas. Provenance records, such as model name, version, prompt, and edit history, are becoming part of responsible disclosure, and the site links to original papers rather than to the Consensus search tool to preserve traceability.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward clearer standards for human-AI co-authorship, machine-readable contribution metadata, and routine disclosure of model use in scholarly and creative work. Authorship may shift from a binary human-only label to layered credit that separates conception, drafting, verification, and accountability. Expect more granular provenance logs and publisher requirements that name the model and the nature of assistance, while unresolved questions about copyright and moral rights continue to be tested. The site's catalogue of 91 AI books and growing paper library will likely track how these norms evolve across disciplines.
